title: SR-Latch
body:
The simplest useful memory circuit, and the base of every other one in
[[Sequential Logic]]. Two cross-coupled NOR gates (or NAND, depending on the version) give
a [[Bi-stable elements|bi-stable element]] with two control inputs: **S**et and **R**eset.

| S | R | $Q_{next}$ | |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|---|
| 0 | 0 | $Q$ | hold: remember what you had |
| 0 | 1 | 0 | reset |
| 1 | 0 | 1 | set |
| 1 | 1 | — | **invalid** |

That last row is the whole reason the [[D-Latch]] exists. $S=R=1$ asks the latch to be set
and reset simultaneously; both outputs go to the same value, $Q$ and $\bar{Q}$ stop being
complements, and releasing both inputs together leaves the circuit
[[metastability|metastable]]. It is not a state you design for, it is a state you design
*out*.

The `hold` row is the interesting one: with both inputs inactive the circuit keeps its
value with no clock, no refresh, and no power beyond keeping the gates on. That is static
memory, and it is what a register is made of.

Add an enable input and you get a gated SR latch; replace S and R with a single data line
so the invalid row is unreachable and you get a [[D-Latch]]. See [[Characteristic Table]]
for how the table above is read forward, and [[Excitation Table]] for reading it backward.
